Overview

Enterprise software doesn't fail from complexity. It fails from fragmentation.

Avantel Defence runs its operations on an internal ERP built by Funwork. Five modules, added over time, each with its own navigation logic, its own patterns, its own assumptions about who the user was. The result was a product that felt like five separate tools stitched together.

The brief was to modernise the system and make it marketable to other manufacturers — tightening the experience for existing users while making it legible enough for a new customer to understand in a demo.

Team: 3 designers · Modules: Production, Marketing, Materials, Stores, Finance · Dashboards: Designed personally

I led the team and took direct ownership of all five module dashboards — the hardest screens, because they needed to answer different questions for different roles without becoming generic.

The challenge

01

Scoping 25 screens

With five modules and 25 screens, every design decision had downstream consequences. Without a locked structure from the start, the project would sprawl. Agreeing on a shared component language before building individual screens was critical to keeping three designers in sync.

02

IA restructure without disruption

The existing navigation was organised by function — every feature listed flat, no grouping logic. Rebuilding the information architecture to match how people actually moved through the product, without breaking familiarity for long-term users, was the core structural challenge.

03

Three users, one system

Operators, floor managers, and the CEO all used the same product. Their data needs diverged sharply. Designing one system that served all three without fragmentation was the defining constraint of the project.

The product

Rather than a process walkthrough, what follows is the actual product — annotated with the decisions that shaped each screen. Five modules, each redesigned from a flat feature list into a role-aware, task-first interface.

01 — Production module
Dashboard overview
The dashboard answers one question first: what is the floor doing right now. Work order status, active shifts, and bottleneck flags surface above the fold. Managers don't need to navigate to find out if production is on track.
Work order detail
Work order detail consolidates part number, quantity, assigned line, materials checklist, and sign-off in one view. Editing and status updates happen in-context — no navigation away from the record.
Status tracking and filters
Status chips (Pending, In Progress, Complete, Delayed) double as one-tap filters. Column sort is persistent — a manager who sorts by delay daily doesn't reset it every session.
02 — Marketing module
Dashboard and pipeline overview
Pipeline stage, lead count per stage, and conversion rate are the three numbers that drive the dashboard. A compact funnel view communicates health faster than a list of records.
Pipeline and lead management
The next action field is required before a lead can advance stages — a light constraint that keeps the pipeline reflecting reality rather than wishful thinking.
Record detail and activity log
Activity log renders calls, emails, and meeting notes in one chronological timeline. No tabs between communication types — context switches kill momentum during a sales follow-up.
03 — Materials module
Inventory dashboard overview
Low-stock alerts and pending requisitions are what a materials manager checks first every morning. Threshold colour indicators mean status is read at a glance, not calculated from a number.
Stock tracking and requisition
Raising a requisition is two steps: select item, confirm quantity and urgency. The previous flow had five steps with redundant confirmation screens. Streamlining the most frequent task reduced daily friction significantly.
Item detail and movement history
Each item record shows stock-in, stock-out, and current location in a chronological log. Audit and operational use share one screen rather than requiring a separate export.
04 — Stores module
Warehouse dashboard overview
Pending GRNs, outward pending, and bay utilisation are the three live numbers a stores manager needs. Dashboard layout mirrors the physical flow of a warehouse: inward left, outward right, current status centre.
Dispatch and inward tracking
GRN creation is inline — scan or enter item codes, confirm quantity against purchase order, flag discrepancies. A discrepancy flag auto-routes to procurement for sign-off. No separate workflow, no email.
GRN and issue record list
Dense rows by default — stores staff deal in high volumes and scan many entries quickly. Date, supplier, and status filters are persistent. Export to PDF is one action from any filtered state.
05 — Finance module
Summary and KPI overview
The finance dashboard is the CEO's primary screen. Five tabs, each answering a different WH question. The tab structure came out of a client constraint — no information should be hidden — and that constraint became the information architecture.
Expenditure breakdown and chart
Bar charts show current vs. prior period side by side. The CEO asked for period comparison after seeing the first iteration with only current-period data. Comparison is the insight; raw numbers are just context.
Transactions and ledger view
Designed for the finance team, not the CEO. Debit/credit columns, voucher numbers, and contra accounts are all visible. Dense, information-forward layout for someone who knows exactly what they're looking for.

Key design decisions

Decision 01 — Navigation
"How do you fix a nav that's grown to list everything?"

The original panel was a flat list of every feature, ordered by when it was built. The new panel groups items by usage frequency: daily tasks at the top, administrative actions collapsed at the bottom, ESOPs last. Frequency, not function, is the right grouping logic for a system people use every day.

Decision 02 — CEO Dashboard
"Should the CEO's dashboard surface everything or filter to what matters?"

The client pushed back against hiding panels. Rather than fight it, tabs were added — each maps to a specific question the CEO needs answered. The structure made the dashboard more coherent, not less. A client constraint, treated as a design brief, produced a better result than the original.

Decision 03 — Shared components
"How do you keep three designers building the same product?"

Before any screens were designed, the team agreed on 12 components: table row, status chip, form field, modal, filter bar. Every screen in all five modules is built from the same set. A locked component language is not a constraint on creativity — it's what makes the product feel like one thing.

Decision 04 — Dashboards
"Same data, three users — how do you design one dashboard that works for all of them?"

You don't. Each dashboard is scoped to the role that owns it. The data overlaps, but what's surfaced first is entirely role-specific. A dashboard that works for everyone works for no one.

What I learned

01
IA before screens saves more time than it costs
Locking navigation structure before designing a single screen felt slow at the start. It turned out to be the project's single biggest time investment. Every screen built after had a clear structural home, which meant rework was about details, not direction. On a 25-screen project with three designers, that coordination paid back in weeks.
02
Pushback from clients is often a problem in disguise
The CEO dashboard tabs came from a client objection. Treating the objection as a design problem — rather than a preference to accommodate — led to a structurally stronger screen. The best decisions on this project came from constraints, not freedom.
03
Data visualisation in enterprise software is still mostly untapped
The dashboards surface numbers and basic charts. Enterprise software historically under-invests in data viz because it's perceived as cosmetic. It isn't — it's the difference between a number and an insight. The next iteration should treat visualisation as a first-class design problem.
